name: Inbox-first, guided workflow
thesis: ERIS is a hand-off machine: a report passes coordinator -> office chief -> branch chief -> engineer -> reviewer -> office chief, and every persona's real question is 'what is waiting on me and what do I press'. The redesign makes that question the whole product: every role lands on a personal Inbox whose rows are named by place (Route 1 PM 12.3, Monterey) and by the verb that moves them forward; every object page (Incident, Assessment, Technical form) opens with one Next-step banner that states the plain status, who owns it, what happens after the action, and the single primary button; and the five hand-offs (triage, delegate, assign, review, finalize) become short route-backed guided flows (2-3 steps, no defaults, consequence stated, confirmation named) instead of dialogs with unlabeled selects. Record browsing (Incidents, Event Groups, Assessments) and the statewide Map remain, but as secondary destinations reached from the Inbox or a small Records area, scoped by default to the user's district or office. Navigation is capped at four destinations per role and renders as a bottom bar on phones, an icon rail on iPads and a sidebar on desktops, so the page content starts within 120px of the top on every device instead of 700px today. Backend objects and the state machine are untouched; only labels change, and each label maps 1:1 to a code.

name: Operations Picture: one map, three layers, act where you stand
thesis: Every ERIS object is a place on the state highway system: a field report, the Event Group it belongs to, the Assessment it spawned and the technical form the engineer writes are all pins at the same Route/Post-Mile. Today the web splits them across seven pages (My Work, Mission Center, Incidents, Event Groups, Assessments, Submissions, Photo evidence) that each show a different slice with a different vocabulary and only two of those pages ever put map and list on screen together (and only at 1440px). The redesign collapses them into one viewport-locked surface, the Map, with three switchable layers (Incidents, Event Groups, Assessments) and one synchronized list. 'Waiting on me' is a filter chip with a count, not a page: turn it on and the map and list show only the pins whose next step belongs to the signed-in person, grouped by what they must do. Selecting a pin or a row opens the same detail panel everywhere (right panel on desktop, drill-in panel on iPad landscape, draggable bottom sheet on phone and iPad portrait) and the workflow action for that step is performed inside the panel through a labelled action sheet, so record-browsing and acting are never two places. Long work leaves the map deliberately: the technical form, terrain tool, intake report and admin consoles are full-screen routes that open pre-centred on the selected site and return to the map at the same pin. A newcomer learns three things in the first minute (the map, the layer chips, the Waiting-on-me count) and everything else is one tap from a pin. Baseline to beat and how: phone content starts at 700px today, on the Map it starts at 56px with the list peeking in the first viewport; My Work is 2.9 screens tall today, the Map is exactly 1.0 with a single scrolling region; the technical form is 11.1 screens with a 532px canvas in a 375px viewport, the new task-list hub is 1.4 screens with zero horizontal overflow; 120 sub-40px tap targets and 74 sub-12px text nodes on that page become 0 by rule.

name: One incident, one case file
thesis: Every ERIS user, whatever their role, is really asking one question: 'what is happening with this incident and what do I do next?' Today the answer is scattered across five numbered objects (Incident #, Event Group #, Assessment #, Submission #, cross-section Project) on six read-only record pages plus a separate action inbox, so a newcomer has to learn the data model before they can do their job. This direction makes the Incident the only object a person navigates to. One role-aware case-file page per incident carries the field report, the Event Group context, the assessment routing (who has it, who is next), every technical form with its evidence, the site map/3D/cross sections, and a single timeline. Backend objects stay exactly as they are; they simply become tabs and cards inside the case file instead of destinations. Lists shrink to simple filterable card lists that open the case file, navigation collapses to Home / Incidents / Map (+ Admin), and every page states plainly where the incident is, who holds it, and what this user can do now. The result beats the measured baseline on every axis: content starts at ~100 px on phones instead of 700 px, no page except a map ever scrolls sideways, the 11-screen-tall 520 px form canvas becomes section pages under two screens each, and every control is 44 px on touch.

name: Radical simplification of what is already there
thesis: ERIS already has the right objects, routes and a working permissions model; what defeats a newcomer is that every page shows everything to everyone, the shell buries content under a 700px navigation card on phones and tablets, and the one long form is a mouse-only pixel canvas. This direction keeps the five destinations, every backend object and every route, and instead removes: each page is cut to the single job it does for the role looking at it, every list becomes a card list below 768px and a priority-column table above it, rail+detail pages become drill-in list-detail below 1024px, the GISA canvas becomes a section hub with a scroll-spy form, autosave and a read-only review mode, every state gets one plain-language label with a 'what happens next' sentence generated from the existing waitingOn() model, and every irreversible action goes through one confirm sheet that also carries the note. Nothing is renamed on the backend; the migration is six phases of mostly layout and component work (about 49 working days) that beats every live baseline: phone content start 700px -> ~104px, technical form 11.1 screens -> per-section pages under 1.5 screens, canvas 532px -> fluid, 120 small tap targets -> 0 on coarse pointers.
